config.editorData:
Resync — how much risk is outstanding, and who is paying for it?

A resync means some data is below the redundancy its policy asks for. Two questions matter and they are different: how much work is left, and what is that work costing the guests.

Zero across the top table is the normal and desirable reading. Nothing is rebuilding, so nothing is at reduced redundancy. The IO columns beside the job counts are there so that a screen of zeros can be told apart from a screen that is not collecting.

If jobs are pending but not running, look at the scheduler table. vSAN deliberately throttles rebuild traffic when guest latency rises, so a deep queue with low parallelism is usually correct behaviour rather than a stall — but it does mean the cluster stays at reduced redundancy for longer, and that is a risk decision somebody should be making knowingly.

Segment cleaning sits at the bottom because on ESA it competes with rebuild work for the same disks.

Reading any column here

A blank cell is not a zero. Where a driver refuses a read, or a rate has no previous sample, this pack emits nothing rather than a zero — because a zero would claim the thing was measured and was fine.

Rate columns are the maximum over the interval, counters marked Raw are cumulative since boot. They are not two views of one number: a Raw column beside its rate is a history beside a present reading, and neither is a duplicate of the other.

Jobs outstanding - the risk

Renders the vSAN Cluster Resync Jobs view.

Num pending resync jobs — Rebuild jobs queued and not yet started. The single best measure of outstanding risk: until this reaches zero, some data is below its intended redundancy.

Num running resync jobs — Rebuild jobs currently executing. vSAN limits concurrency deliberately, so a large pending count with a small running count is normal pacing, not a stall.

Num suspended resync jobs — Rebuild jobs vSAN has paused, usually to protect guest IO. Sustained non-zero here with a non-zero pending count means rebuilds are not progressing, and the cluster is staying at reduced redundancy longer than it needs to.

Num inflight priority resync jobs — Rebuilds vSAN has prioritised, which it does when data is at genuine risk rather than merely non-compliant.

Num inflight shared resync jobs — Rebuilds running at normal priority.

Num pending decom resync jobs — Rebuilds queued because a host or disk is being evacuated. Non-zero means a maintenance operation is waiting on data movement.

Num pending full resync jobs — Queued rebuilds that must copy a whole component rather than a delta. These are the expensive ones.

Num running full resync jobs — Full-component rebuilds currently running.

Resync parallelism (average) — How many rebuild operations vSAN is running at once on average. Low parallelism with a deep pending queue is the signature of throttling.

Num complete resync ops — Lifetime count of completed rebuild operations. Cumulative since boot; the trend tells you whether progress is being made.

Num complete full resync ops — Lifetime count of completed full-component rebuilds.

Resync Read IOPS — Read operations per second performed to rebuild redundancy. Zero unless something is actually resyncing, which is the normal and desirable reading.

Recovery Write IOPS — Write operations per second performed to restore redundancy -- the other half of a rebuild.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Rebuild IO rates

Renders the vSAN Cluster Resync view.

Resync Read IOPS — Read operations per second performed to rebuild redundancy. Zero unless something is actually resyncing, which is the normal and desirable reading.

Resync Read Throughput — Bytes per second read for rebuild.

Resync Read Lat — Average latency of rebuild reads.

Recovery Write IOPS — Write operations per second performed to restore redundancy -- the other half of a rebuild.

Recovery Write Throughput — Bytes per second written to restore redundancy. Divide the outstanding work by this to estimate how long a rebuild has left.

Recovery Write Lat — Average latency of recovery writes.

Back end during rebuild

Renders the vSAN Cluster DOM Component Manager view.

Read Lat — Average read latency at this layer. Broadcom's own threshold for this metric is 15 ms warning and 30 ms critical, published in the Performance Service graph definition as yellow=15000 red=30000 microseconds, direction upper. That is a badly-wrong line rather than a tuning line -- a healthy cluster here runs under 1.5 ms, so the product only flags at roughly ten times normal. Compare the same column across the client, owner and component manager views: the layer where the number first becomes large is the layer to investigate.

Write Lat — Average write latency at this layer. On ESA a write is acknowledged after it is logged, so this is usually far lower than the component manager's figure beneath it. Product threshold 15 ms warning, 30 ms critical.

Congestions — vSAN's own backpressure signal, raised when a layer cannot absorb the offered load and asks the layer above to slow down. Zero on a healthy cluster, and it reads zero here. Any sustained non-zero value is the single most important number on the screen.

OIO — Outstanding IO: operations issued and not yet completed. Latency multiplied by nothing tells you why it is high -- this does. High latency with high outstanding IO is queueing, high latency with low outstanding IO is a slow device.

Read IOPS — Read operations per second. Always read beside latency: high latency at high IOPS is a busy VM, high latency at near-zero IOPS is a sick one.

Write IOPS — Write operations per second.

Segment cleaning

Renders the vSAN Segment Cleaning Per Host view.

IOPS seg cleaner unmap — Operations per second performed by the segment cleaner. ESA writes to a log and must later reclaim partially-used segments; this is that housekeeping, and it competes with guest IO for the same disks.

Lat avg seg cleaner unmap — Average latency of segment cleaning work.

Lat max seg cleaner unmap — Worst segment cleaning latency in the interval. Measured at 370 milliseconds here against a 1.3 millisecond average. Housekeeping stalling for a third of a second is worth knowing about, and no other screen in this pack would show it.

Lat stddev seg cleaner unmap — Spread of segment cleaning latency.

Throughput seg cleaner unmap — Bytes per second the segment cleaner is moving. This is write amplification made visible: capacity the disks are spending on vSAN's own bookkeeping rather than on guest data.

Seg clean unmap leaf owner max lat µs — Worst average latency any single replica contributed to segment cleaning. Isolates one bad disk inside an otherwise healthy cleaning cycle.

Unmap IOPS — Space-reclamation operations per second, including those originated by guests trimming their filesystems.

Unmap Lat — Average latency of unmap operations.

Lat max unmap — Worst unmap latency in the interval.

Unmap count — Lifetime count of unmap operations. Cumulative since boot.
